To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(i) interest groups can control the agenda in the legislative process, and (ii) this control can lead to convergence to the median legislator.

(1) convergence to the median of the legislature is possible, but not necessarily so, (2) the speed of convergence depends on the patience of the interest groups, (3) convergence can be faster if only one side of policy is organized.
(i) convergence is faster when only business interest groups are organized, and that (ii) convergence is slowest when all interest groups are organized and they have infinite patience.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how the agenda formation process among interest groups affects the dynamic policy-making process.
the role of interest group organization in the policy making process.
the question of how the agenda setting power of organized interests affects the speed of policy convergence in a legislature.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
interest group organization may lead to a more stable policy, but not always, and may even lead to more policy oscillation if interest groups are not patient enough.
the speed of convergence is determined by both the patience of interest groups and the number of interest groups representing the right and left sides of the policy space.
the speed of convergence depends on the number of interest groups, their patience and the number of policy dimensions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the degree of convergence to the median legislatorʼs ideal point in our model is a function of the degree of organization and the patience of interest groups.
interest groups can affect policy outcomes by controlling the agenda, but the impact of their control is not necessarily monotone.
interest groups may be able to influence the policy process even in the absence of any explicit lobbying activity.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the presence of interest groups can slow or even halt convergence to the median of the legislature.
interest groups can be a powerful force in shaping the legislative process, even if they have no formal role in the legislative body.
interest groups can be an impediment to the median voterʼs ideal policy being implemented.
